name: GAAP principles
subject: Accounting
example_problem: A business bought land for R500 000 in 2019; it is now worth R900 000 but is still shown at R500 000. Name and explain the GAAP principle applied, then match four more scenarios to prudence, materiality, business entity and going concern.
prior_knowledge: Basic accounting concepts: assets, liabilities, income, expenses

importance.summary: Applied in every financial-reporting answer on Paper 1 (150 marks) - statements questions expect entries justified by principle (prudence, matching, going concern...).

covered_by.subtopic: GAAP principles: historical cost, prudence, materiality, business entity rule, going concern, matching

diagnostic.prompt: Land bought for R500 000 in 2019 is now worth R900 000 but still shown at R500 000. The GAAP principle applied is:
The owner pays their home electricity from the business bank account and it is recorded as Drawings. The principle applied is:

recap:
GAAP - Generally Accepted Accounting Practice - is the shared rulebook that makes financial statements trustworthy and comparable. Grade 10 needs six principles, and exams almost never ask for definitions: they give a scenario and ask which principle is applied. So learn each rule with its tell-tale sign.

Historical cost: assets are recorded at their original, verifiable purchase price, not today's estimated value. The purchase price is a fact backed by a source document; market value is a shifting opinion. Sign: an asset "now worth more" but "still shown at" what it cost.

Prudence: never overstate good news, never understate bad news - anticipate possible losses, never record profits before they are certain. Writing off doubtful debts and valuing damaged stock at the lower figure are prudence at work. Sign: a cautious choice made under uncertainty. Do not confuse it with historical cost: historical cost sticks to an original price; prudence picks the careful estimate when the outcome is uncertain.

Materiality: information is material if leaving it out or misstating it would change a reader's decision. A R45 stapler that lasts years is simply expensed - too small to matter - while a delivery vehicle is a fixed asset tracked separately. Sign: a decision turning on whether an amount is big enough to matter.

Business entity rule: the business and its owner are separate in the books. The owner's personal spending from business funds is Drawings, never a business expense; the owner's private car and house never appear among business assets. Sign: any brush between the owner's personal affairs and the business records - "the owner took", "for personal use".

Going concern: the books assume the business will keep operating into the foreseeable future - which justifies recording assets at cost for continued use and spreading costs over future years. Sign: statements prepared "assuming the business will continue".

Matching: incomes and expenses belong to the period in which they occur, so a period's expenses are matched against that period's income for a fair profit. Insurance paid in advance is split between years; wages owed at year end are accrued into the year they were worked. Sign: amounts shifted between periods - prepaid, accrued, "belongs to this year".

Exam method: underline the action taken, then ask what the accountant is refusing to do or insisting on doing. The refusal points straight at the principle.

exit_check.prompt: A business writes down damaged stock to below cost while ignoring a rumoured increase in its land's value. The principle is:
options: Prudence - anticipate losses, never anticipate profits

exit_check.prompt: Insurance of R12 000 paid in March for 12 months, with a June year end, is split so only four months count as this year's expense. The principle is:
What single question best identifies the principle in any scenario?
options: What is the accountant refusing to do, or insisting on doing?
